questions.q: Newton's First Law of Motion is also called the Law of Inertia. What is the inertia of an object?
options: A force that keeps a moving object moving
Its tendency to resist changes to its motion, depending only on its mass
The net force required to keep it at constant velocity
The friction that slows a coin sliding across a table
questions.explanation: Inertia is not a force; it is a property of all objects, namely the tendency to resist changes to its motion, and it depends only on the object's mass. An object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless made to change by a non-zero net force.

questions.q: A rowing team's boat is propelled forward by the oars. Using Newton's Third Law of Motion, explain why the boat moves forward.
options: The oars reduce the weight of the boat so it floats forward
As each oar pushes back on the water, the water pushes back with an equal and opposite force on the oar
The water has no effect; the rowers' inertia carries the boat forward
The normal reaction force of the water lifts the boat forward
questions.explanation: By Newton's Third Law, as the face of each oar pushes back on the water, the water pushes back with an equal and opposite force on each oar, propelling the rowers and their boat forward. The action and reaction forces act on different objects, so they never cancel.

questions.q: A 60 kg trolley rolls down a slope inclined at 30 degrees. Its weight is mg = 588 N and a friction force of 270 N acts up the slope. Find the trolley's acceleration down the slope.
working: Component of weight parallel to slope: \(W_{//} = mg\sin 30^\circ = 588 \times 0.5 = 294\,\mathrm{N}\)
questions.explanation: Resolve the weight along the slope as mg sin 30°, subtract friction to get the net force, then divide by the mass. The full weight (588 N) is never used along the slope — only the parallel component (294 N).

questions.q: A 30 kg child on a swing descends through a vertical height of 2.0 m. Using the Law of Conservation of Energy, find the child's speed at the lowest point of the swing (take g = 9.8).
working: By conservation of energy, the loss in gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy: \(mg\Delta h = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\)
questions.explanation: Any loss in gravitational potential energy (Ug = mgh) equals the gain in kinetic energy, so mgΔh = ½mv². The mass cancels in the working, so the speed depends only on the vertical height dropped, not on the child's mass.

questions.q: A car's kinetic energy is given by Ek = ½mv². What happens to its kinetic energy if its speed (velocity) is doubled?
options: It stays the same because the mass is unchanged
It doubles
It produces a fourfold increase in the kinetic energy
It increases eightfold
questions.explanation: Because kinetic energy depends on the square of the velocity, a doubling of velocity produces a fourfold increase in the kinetic energy — and therefore a fourfold increase in the work needed to stop the car. This is why 'speed kills': stopping distance grows with the square of the speed.

questions.q: The textbook defines the momentum, p, of an object. Which statement correctly describes momentum?
options: The product of an object's mass and its acceleration, a scalar measured in newtons
The product of an object's mass and its velocity, a vector measured in N s or kg m s⁻¹
The force exerted during a collision, measured in joules
The change in an object's velocity over the time of a collision
questions.explanation: The product of an object's mass and its velocity is its momentum, p. Momentum is a vector quantity and is measured in either newton seconds (N s) or kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹). Impulse, by contrast, is the change in momentum (FΔt = mΔv).

questions.q: From memory: how do vehicle safety features such as crumple zones, seatbelts and airbags reduce the net force on a human body during a collision?
keyPoints: The impulse delivered by the net force equals the change in momentum of the body: FΔt = mΔv.
For a given change in momentum, increasing the time interval Δt over which the momentum changes decreases the net force F.
Crumple zones, seatbelts and airbags are designed to increase this time interval, so the force on the body is reduced ('extend the time, cut the force').
questions.explanation: If you stated FΔt = mΔv and linked a longer collision time to a smaller force, grade yourself Good or Easy. The change in momentum is fixed by the speeds, so the only lever is the contact time.

questions.q: A 2000 kg delivery van collides with a stationary 1000 kg car. The two vehicles lock together and the tangled wreck moves off at 20 m s⁻¹. Using conservation of momentum, find the speed of the van just before the collision.
working: Conservation of momentum: \(\Sigma p_{after} = \Sigma p_{before} = m_{van}u_{van} + m_{car}u_{car}\)
questions.explanation: Total momentum before equals total momentum after. The stationary car contributes zero momentum before, so all the momentum after (60 000 kg m s⁻¹) came from the van, giving 30 m s⁻¹. This 'lock-together' collision is inelastic — momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.

questions.q: Two objects collide and the total kinetic energy before the collision is greater than the total kinetic energy after. How is this collision classified, and what is conserved?
options: Elastic; both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Inelastic; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not conserved
Elastic; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
Inelastic; neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
questions.explanation: If the kinetic energy before is greater than the kinetic energy after, kinetic energy is not conserved, therefore the collision is inelastic. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved; momentum is conserved in every collision regardless of type.

questions.q: From memory: the module gives three tools for any mechanics problem — forces, energy and momentum. State which tool you should reach for first in each situation.
keyPoints: Use Newton's laws and forces when you need an acceleration, a force, a normal or friction force, or anything involving time, and on inclined planes.
Use energy when the problem involves heights and speeds with no mention of time, or asks about work, power or energy transformed.
Use momentum for any collision, explosion or recoil, and pair it with an energy comparison to classify the collision as elastic or inelastic.
All three approaches are linked and must agree, so a second method is a powerful check.
questions.explanation: If you matched collision/explosion to momentum, heights-and-speeds-without-time to energy, and force/acceleration/time to Newton's laws, grade yourself Good or Easy. The work-energy theorem and impulse are just Newton's second law integrated over distance and over time.
